sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A network can be connected and still perform badly. Connect each reported symptom to the most likely network condition.
bullets: Slow network speeds and limited connectivity
sections.callout: CONNECTIVITY → PERFORMANCE → TIMING → SIGNAL → AUTHENTICATION → INTERNET

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a user reports disconnects, slowness, delayed traffic, bad VoIP, wireless interference, or login problems, identify the symptom and where to investigate.
bullets: Wi-Fi drops and reconnects → intermittent wireless
Switch port cycles up/down → port flapping
Internet disappears and returns → intermittent internet

sections.title: Common Network Symptoms
paragraphs: Several problems can feel like the network is simply bad. Identify how it is failing: connectivity, performance, timing, physical link, radio environment, authentication, or upstream internet.
sections.callout: Describe the failure precisely before troubleshooting it.

sections.title: Intermittent Wireless Connectivity
paragraphs: Wi-Fi that disconnects, reconnects, loses signal, or works only periodically can result from weak signal, interference, congestion, an access point, the client adapter, movement, or range.
sections.callout: Laptop Wi-Fi drops while wired systems remain stable → intermittent wireless connectivity.

sections.title: Wireless Signal and Distance
paragraphs: Wireless signals weaken with greater distance, obstacles, and interference. A problem limited to one physical area strongly suggests coverage or interference.
sections.callout: LOCATION MATTERS → SIGNAL OR INTERFERENCE.

sections.title: Slow Network Speeds
paragraphs: Congestion, weak wireless signal, interference, damaged cabling, hardware limits, network saturation, or provider trouble can reduce throughput even while the connection remains active.
sections.callout: CONNECTED, BUT SLOW.

sections.title: Speed vs. Latency

table.caption: Throughput and delay
rows: How much data moves over time
How long data takes to travel or respond

sections.callout: High bandwidth can coexist with noticeable latency.

sections.title: Limited Connectivity
paragraphs: Limited connectivity means a device can reach some network resources but not everything it should. Investigate IP configuration, gateway, DNS, DHCP, and network access.
sections.callout: Local network works but external networks do not → check gateway and connectivity configuration.

sections.title: Jitter
paragraphs: Jitter is variation in packet delay. Inconsistent arrival timing is especially noticeable in VoIP, video calls, and streaming.
sections.callout: Packet delay changes from one packet to the next → jitter.

sections.title: High Latency
paragraphs: Latency is the delay between sending data and receiving a response. High latency causes lag, delayed responses, and noticeable conversation delay.
sections.callout: High latency = wait.

sections.title: Poor VoIP Quality
paragraphs: VoIP problems can sound choppy, delayed, robotic, broken, or full of dropouts. Jitter, latency, packet loss, congestion, and insufficient network performance are common contributors.
sections.callout: VoIP exposes timing problems quickly.

sections.title: VoIP and Jitter
paragraphs: Voice packets need predictable timing. Significant variation makes audio choppy or uneven.
sections.callout: JITTER → CHOPPY VOICE.

sections.title: VoIP and Latency
paragraphs: Packets that consistently take too long create conversational delay. Choppy or uneven audio points toward jitter; a long delay points toward latency.
sections.callout: LATENCY → DELAYED VOICE.

sections.title: Port Flapping
paragraphs: Port flapping occurs when a switch port repeatedly transitions up, down, up, and down. Faulty cabling, connectors, a NIC, the switch port, or other physical-link instability can cause it.
sections.callout: Switch logs show one interface cycling repeatedly → port flapping.

sections.title: External Interference
paragraphs: Other Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth devices, microwave ovens, and RF-producing equipment can disrupt wireless communication.
sections.callout: Wi-Fi becomes unreliable when nearby RF equipment operates → external interference.

sections.title: Interference vs. Weak Signal
sections.callout: A Wi-Fi analyzer can help inspect the radio environment.

sections.title: Authentication Failures
paragraphs: Incorrect or expired credentials, a wrong wireless key, certificate trouble, account restrictions, or authentication-server problems can prevent a user or device from proving its identity.
sections.callout: Network exists, but credentials are rejected → authentication failure.

table.caption: Identity and network path
rows: Identity check rejects the user or device
Required network path cannot be established

sections.title: Intermittent Internet Connectivity
paragraphs: External internet access that repeatedly works, stops, and returns can involve the ISP, modem or ONT, router, WAN cabling, DNS in some scenarios, or an unstable upstream service.
sections.callout: Determine whether the local network also fails.

sections.title: Local Network vs. Internet
paragraphs: If local servers and printers remain reachable while websites fail, focus on the gateway, WAN, or ISP. If the entire local connection disappears, investigate local networking first.
sections.callout: LAN WORKS + INTERNET FAILS → LOOK OUTWARD.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Data transfers slowly → slow network speed
Choppy IP call → poor VoIP quality
Switch interface cycles up/down → port flapping
Nearby RF disrupts wireless → external interference
Internet disappears and returns → intermittent internet

sections.title: Objective 5.5 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Several symptoms feel like the network is bad. Identify exactly how it is failing.

entries.title: Slow Speed vs. High Latency
paragraphs: Slow speed means low throughput; high latency means long response time.

entries.title: Latency vs. Jitter
paragraphs: Latency is delay; jitter is variation in delay.

entries.title: Jitter vs. Poor VoIP
paragraphs: Jitter is a network condition; poor VoIP is the experience it can help cause.

entries.title: Intermittent Wireless vs. Internet
paragraphs: A Wi-Fi path that drops is wireless trouble. Wi-Fi that stays connected while internet access disappears points toward WAN or provider trouble.

entries.title: Limited Connectivity vs. Authentication
paragraphs: Limited connectivity provides incomplete access; authentication rejects identity or credentials.

entries.title: Port Flapping vs. Wireless Disconnects
paragraphs: Port flapping affects a wired switch interface; intermittent wireless affects the radio connection.

entries.title: Weak Signal vs. External Interference
paragraphs: Distance and obstacles weaken signal; competing RF sources create interference.

sections.title: Network Troubleshooting Workflow
bullets: Identify whether connectivity is wired, wireless, local, or internet-facing.
Separate throughput from delay and changing delay.
Use VoIP symptoms to distinguish jitter and latency clues.
Inspect switch logs for port-state changes.
Compare wireless coverage with external RF activity.
Separate access-path failure from credential rejection.
sections.callout: CONNECTIVITY → PERFORMANCE → TIMING → SIGNAL → AUTHENTICATION → INTERNET
